title: Asking how someone is
body: A polite everyday greeting.

title: Saying hello
body: The standard greeting all day until evening. Say it when you enter a shop. Sounds like 'bon-ZHOOR'.
example_sentence: Bonjour, je voudrais du pain, s'il vous plaît.

title: A casual 'how are you?'
body: Informal, for friends and family. The answer can be the same words: 'Ça va !' (I'm fine!).

title: Nice to meet you
body: Said when meeting someone. Written 'enchantée' by a woman; it sounds the same. Sounds like 'on-shon-TAY'.

title: Saying please
body: The polite form. With friends you can say 's'il te plaît'.

title: Thank you very much
body: The 'r' in merci is soft, from the throat. Reply to thanks with 'de rien' (you're welcome).

title: When you don't understand
body: Very useful for learners. 'Ne' is often dropped in speech: 'Je comprends pas'.

title: Asking someone to repeat
body: Polite and useful. You can add 'plus lentement' (more slowly).
example_sentence: Pouvez-vous répéter plus lentement, s'il vous plaît ?

title: Finding the toilets
body: Always plural in French: 'les toilettes'.

title: Asking the price
body: Essential at the market.

title: Ordering politely
body: 'Je voudrais' (I would like) is more polite than 'je veux' (I want).
term: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît
translation: I would like a coffee, please
example_sentence: Je voudrais un café et un croissant, s'il vous plaît.

title: Getting attention
body: Use it to stop someone politely or to say sorry for a small thing.

title: Introducing yourself
body: Literally 'I call myself'.

title: See you soon
body: A friendly goodbye when you expect to meet again.

title: Have a good day
body: Said when leaving a shop or ending a call. In the evening say 'bonne soirée'.

title: Agreeing
body: Very common in conversation. Sounds like 'dah-KOR'.
example_sentence: On se voit à midi ? D'accord.

title: Asking the time
body: The answer starts with 'Il est...': 'Il est trois heures' (It is three o'clock).

title: Saying sorry
body: Written 'désolée' by a woman. For a small bump, 'pardon' is enough.
example_sentence: Je suis désolé, je suis en retard.

title: Asking about English
body: Useful when you are stuck.

title: Enjoy your meal
body: Said before eating. English borrowed the phrase too.
example_sentence: Le dîner est prêt. Bon appétit !

title: Word: le travail
body: Masculine noun. The verb is 'travailler' (to work).
example_sentence: Je vais au travail en bus.

title: Word: la maison
body: Feminine noun. 'À la maison' means at home.
example_sentence: Je reste à la maison ce soir.

title: Word: l'eau
body: Feminine noun. Sounds like 'LOH'. Tap water: 'l'eau du robinet'.
example_sentence: Une bouteille d'eau, s'il vous plaît.

title: Word: aujourd'hui
body: One of the most useful time words. Sounds like 'oh-zhoor-DWEE'.

title: Word: demain
body: Pairs with 'hier' (yesterday) and 'aujourd'hui' (today).

title: Word: hier
body: Sounds like 'ee-YAIR'.

title: Word: la gare
body: Feminine noun. A bus station is 'la gare routière'.
example_sentence: La gare est à dix minutes à pied.

title: Word: l'argent
body: Masculine noun. It also means the metal silver.

title: Word: le marché
body: Masculine noun. 'Faire le marché' means to do the market shopping.
example_sentence: Le marché ouvre à sept heures.

title: Tu or vous?
body: 'Tu' is informal 'you' for friends, family and children. 'Vous' is polite 'you' for strangers, older people and at work, and also plural 'you'. When unsure, use 'vous'.

title: Every noun has a gender
body: French nouns are masculine (le) or feminine (la). Before a vowel both become l'. Plural is always les. Learn each noun with its article: le livre (book), la table (table).

title: Silent final letters
body: Final consonants are usually silent: 'petit' sounds like 'puh-TEE', 'Paris' like 'pah-REE'. Often the letters c, r, f and l are pronounced at the end, as in 'avec', 'bonjour', 'neuf', 'mal'.

title: Linking words: liaison
body: A silent final consonant is often pronounced when the next word starts with a vowel. 'Les amis' sounds like 'lay-za-MEE', and 'vous avez' like 'voo-za-VAY'.

title: Making a sentence negative
body: Wrap the verb with 'ne ... pas'. 'Je parle' (I speak) becomes 'Je ne parle pas' (I don't speak). Before a vowel, 'ne' becomes 'n'': 'Je n'aime pas'.

title: Counting from 70 to 99
body: French counts 70 as 'sixty-ten' (soixante-dix), 80 as 'four-twenties' (quatre-vingts) and 90 as 'four-twenty-ten' (quatre-vingt-dix). In Belgium and Switzerland, 70 is 'septante' and 90 is 'nonante'.

title: Please or thanks?
body: Everyday French.
explanation: 'Merci' means thank you. 'Please' is 's'il vous plaît' (formal) or 's'il te plaît' (informal).

title: The book
body: Basic vocabulary.
explanation: 'Le livre' is the book. Careful: 'la livre' means a pound (weight or money).

title: Polite 'you'
body: Tu or vous?
statement: 'Vous' is used for the polite or formal 'you'
explanation: 'Vous' is polite and also plural. 'Tu' is for people you know well.

title: French numbers
body: Counting check.

title: Evening greeting
body: Greetings check.
explanation: Use 'bonsoir' from late afternoon. 'Bonne nuit' (good night) is only for going to bed.

title: Cat or dog?
body: Animal words.
explanation: 'Le chat' is the cat and 'le chien' is the dog.

title: Saying goodbye
body: Everyday French.
explanation: 'Au revoir' literally means 'until we see again'.
